Peace Sign
PEES SYN
noun (Boomer slang)
Two signs share the name. The peace symbol — a circle enclosing a vertical line and two lines angled downward — was designed in February 1958 by the British artist Gerald Holtom for a march against nuclear weapons, combining the semaphore signals for N and D ("nuclear disarmament"); it was adopted by the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and spread to the American civil-rights and anti-Vietnam movements in the 1960s. The peace sign gesture — two fingers raised in a V — was Winston Churchill’s "V for Victory" in 1941, re-read as "peace" by the 1960s counterculture.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The peace sign is both a gesture — two fingers in a V — and a symbol — the circle with the downward lines — and to Boomers it meant the whole anti-war, anti-nuke, love-and-peace hope of the 1960s. Grandchildren still flash it in photos without a thought. The Christian observation: the sign promised peace and could not give it; Scripture names the One who can. The gesture began as Churchill’s V for victory in a war against real evil, and the 1960s turned it into a plea for peace by disarmament. Both are signs pointing at something beyond themselves. Scripture’s sign of peace is a Person: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given ... and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6). His peace is a different kind: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you" (Joh 14:27). It is first peace with God, "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1), and then peace between enemies: "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us" (Eph 2:14). And it was made at a cost the 1960s never reckoned with: "having made peace through the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). The Christian’s peace sign is the cross. A child who flashes two fingers for a photo is not sinning; but his parents can show him the sign that actually delivers what it promises.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer emblem of 1960s peace and disarmament — Holtom’s 1958 nuclear-disarmament symbol and Churchill’s V gesture re-read as "peace" — a sign of a hope Scripture fulfils only in the Prince of Peace, who made peace through the blood of His cross (Col 1:20).

PEACE SIGN, n. (Boomer era, 1960s–) 1. A hand gesture with the index and middle fingers raised in a V, palm outward, signifying peace (earlier, Churchill’s "V for Victory," 1941). 2. The peace symbol, a circle enclosing a vertical stroke and two downward diagonals, designed by Gerald Holtom (1958) for the nuclear-disarmament movement.

Webster (1828) — SIGN, noun [Latin signum; Gr. deicnumt.] 1. A token; something by which another thing is shown or represented; any visible thing, any motion, appearance or event which indicates the existence or approach of something else. Thus we speak of signs of fair weather or of a storm, and of external marks which are signs of a good constitution. 2. A motion, action, nod or gesture indicating a wish or command. They made signs to his father, how he would have him called. Luke 1:62 . 3. A wonder; a miracle; a prodigy; a remarkable transaction, event or phenomenon. Through mighty signs and wonders. Romans 15:19 . Luke 1:62 1.

Decode for families: in a selfie, two fingers usually mean "hi." Tell your children what it meant in 1968, and what the cross means always.

Key Scripture

Isa 9:6 — "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."

Joh 14:27 — "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."

Rom 5:1 — "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:"

Eph 2:14 — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;"

Col 1:20 — "And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven."

Modern Corruption

The peace sign stood for a peace sought by protest and disarmament; Scripture offers a peace that is a Person, made first between God and man through the blood of the cross.

expand to see more

Symbols carry hopes, and the peace sign carried a generation’s hope that war could be ended by refusing to fight. The hope was sincere and the fear of nuclear war was rational. But the peace movement’s peace had no account of why men fight, and so no cure for it. James had already given the diagnosis: wars come from the lusts that war in our members. A sign on a placard cannot reach that far down.

The gospel’s peace begins at the root. It reconciles the sinner to God (Rom 5:1), and only then reconciles enemies to each other (Eph 2:14). The world gives peace by treaty and slogan; Christ gives it "not as the world giveth" (Joh 14:27) — by His own death. That is why the church’s symbol is not a circle with lines but a cross.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin pax + Latin signum (a mark, a token) → 1941 Churchill’s V sign → 1958 Holtom’s peace symbol (semaphore N + D) → 1960s counterculture peace sign.

expand to see more

Latin pax — peace; signum — a mark, token, standard

1941: Winston Churchill popularizes the V-for-Victory gesture

February 1958: Gerald Holtom designs the nuclear-disarmament symbol (semaphore N and D)

Easter 1958: first carried on the march to Aldermaston, England

1960s: adopted by the American anti-war movement and counterculture
